rv.q: Anjana Vasan gives an electrifying central performance in this lean, focused and visually arresting drama about PTSD
At points, you'll forget that this one is scripted, so natural are their shifts between easy charm and insecure rage.
But the self-consciousness of Forsyth’s writing is a struggle.

All of it feels incredibly real and dangerous. Daniel Raggett’s direction is snappy too, carrying both playfulness and threat over the course of the drama. But the couple are unconvincing, and so are the forced moral dilemmas in Forsyth’s script, although the performances are compelling, particularly Vasan’s.

That vertiginous feeling underpins every bracing moment of Brace Brace, the lean, mean, 75-minute play from Oli Forsyth that follows on from Giant in once again making the Royal Court a theatrical must.
Luckily, the outstanding performances and production make Brace Brace an engaging and thrilling watch.
A play not for the faint-hearted, and especially those fearful of flying
But in the end Brace Brace is just a work in progress.
More work is needed but this is still an exhilarating evening.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this nerve-shredding hijacking drama: some praise its thrilling staging and immersive terror, while others find the premise more compelling than its execution of trauma's aftermath.
